planting.note: Tuck rooted offsets at an angle into rock crevices or a steep, fast-draining slope in spring, keeping the gray-green rosette itself clear of standing soil or mulch to prevent crown rot.

directions: Plant at a slight angle in a rocky cliff face, dry stone wall, or steep clay slope with sharp drainage, mimicking the canyon and foothill outcrops this California and southern Oregon native calls home. Compact gray-green rosettes send up wiry, erect stems of bright red-orange to yellow star-shaped flowers in late spring, drawing hummingbirds even in a small rock garden planting. Water sparingly and only during active growth in winter and spring; once summer heat arrives the rosettes should be left completely dry, as the species is adapted to a long dormant season with essentially no irrigation. Give it partial shade on hot inland sites or full sun near the coast, and avoid any soil that holds moisture around the fleshy leaves.

planting.note: Set small offset clusters into rocky outcrop crevices or a lean, gritty raised bed in spring, leaving the compact rosette perched above grade so the central caudex never sits in wet soil.

directions: Grow in shallow rocky soil pockets, outcrops, or a lean scree bed that drains instantly after rain, reflecting the chaparral, foothill woodland, and open rock habitats where this California and northern Baja native is found. Small, thick-leaved gray-green rosettes cluster slowly around a woody base and send up branching stalks of small pale yellow star-shaped flowers in late spring. Water lightly during the cool winter and spring growing season and withhold water almost entirely through summer dormancy, since the species is highly sensitive to rot from excess moisture at the root crown. It is well suited to a rock garden crevice, trough, or container of mineral, fast-draining mix where it can be viewed up close.

planting.note: Plant small rosette offsets on an angled rocky slope or in a shallow clay-soil pocket in spring, choosing a spot with excellent runoff since this coastal species is especially prone to rot in heavy or wet soil.

directions: Site in thin rocky or clay soil on a sunny coastal slope or bluff with sharp drainage, matching the chaparral and coastal scrub habitat of this San Diego-to-Santa-Barbara-County and Baja California native. Narrow, pointed, cone-shaped succulent leaves form small erect rosettes that send up slender branching stalks of pale yellow star-shaped flowers in spring. Water only sparingly during winter rains and keep completely dry through the long summer dormancy, since the species is adapted to months without rainfall and quickly succumbs to rot in damp conditions. It is best grown in a rock garden, dry wall, or shallow container of mineral succulent mix rather than a conventional garden bed.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container divisions in spring into lean, fast-draining soil mixed with coarse sand or pumice in full sun; this Orostachys spreads quickly into a carpet of rosettes once established.

directions: Plant in nutritionally poor, sharply drained soil amended with extra grit in full sun, matching the rocky outcrops of its native range across Siberia, China, Korea, and Japan. This species forms low, dense clumps of soft gray-green rosettes that spread readily by offsets to carpet a rock garden, trough, or gravel bed, with mature rosettes sending up a conical spike of small whitish flowers before fading back while surrounding offsets carry the colony forward. It is fully dormant in winter, dying back to resting buds at the soil surface and returning reliably in spring, and tolerates both summer drought and cold winters far better than it tolerates wet, poorly drained soil. Water sparingly, letting the soil dry fully between waterings.
